title: 'It's hard not to believe in ghosts working at this pub - now this confirms it'
excerpt: Ghost hunters believe one of Kent’s oldest pubs is filled with restless spirits after being asked to investigate supernatural sightings.
content:
Ghost hunters believe one of Kent’s oldest pubs is filled with restless spirits after investigating repeated sightings and the building’s murky history.

Staff at the Royal Victoria and Bull Hotel in Dartford invited an experienced team of paranormal investigators in following years of unexplained activity reported by employees and customers.

Witnesses visiting at different times have described the same figures appearing in the same rooms, including a man in an old fashioned hat and another who watches guests from a bedroom corner.

Lucy, who has worked at the Royal Victoria and Bull for 17 years, said she once caught a fleeting glimpse of the dark figure before he suddenly disappeared.

Asked whether she believed the hotel was haunted, she told KentOnline: “How can we not believe in ghosts? For 17 years, people have been telling us the same stories.

“They don’t know one another, yet they describe the same figures appearing in the same rooms.”

Several people have described seeing a man in the same bedroom, sometimes sitting near the bed and sometimes observing its occupants from a corner.

Staff have nicknamed the recurring figure “the watcher”.

Her colleague Kirsty had already heard the stories when she caught a brief glimpse of a man sitting on the edge of a bed.

“He was there for a split second and then he was gone,” she said.

“His presence can feel intimidating, but I think he likes women,” she said. “Perhaps he is watching over them.”

Sue Marshall and her daughter Vicky are members of The Paranormal Inspectres, a team of investigators with more than 25 years’ experience examining unexplained activity.

But their interest is not limited to just finding ghosts.

They research the history of each building and consider whether unusual sounds, movements or sensations could have a natural explanation.

Sue said the Royal Victoria and Bull proved particularly fascinating because similar figures had been reported in the same rooms by people visiting at different times.

The group spent two nights inside the hotel, moving between its bedrooms, bars, function room and cellar until the early hours.

Although Sue is accustomed to entering supposedly haunted buildings, there was one part of the hotel where even she would not have wanted to spend the night.

“I wouldn’t go up in that room,” she said of room 103, where investigators had been told about an angry male presence.

A camera left there captured a ball of light moving across the room.

After enlarging a still from the footage, the group believed it contained the shape of a face.

Vicky also sensed what she described as an angry man pacing through the room and telling people what to do.

The investigators placed cameras and voice recorders in bedrooms and bars to capture anything they might miss during the day.

Their equipment included motion sensors, thermal cameras to identify changes in temperature and K2 meters, small handheld devices which light up when they detect fluctuations in electromagnetic fields.

To attempt direct communication, the group used an Ouija board, where a glass moves between letters, and dowsing rods, which cross or change direction in response to questions.

A pen planchette allowed a pen to move across paper beneath the hands of those taking part.

Inside the bedroom associated with the watcher, K2 meters repeatedly lit up while female investigators asked questions.

Two sets of dowsing rods appeared to move in the same way and provide matching answers.

A camera left inside the closed room captured several unexplained balls of light, known among paranormal investigators as orbs.

When one was enlarged, the investigators believed they could see the shape of a face within it.

The equipment could not reveal the watcher’s identity, but the hotel’s history offers no shortage of former occupants who might still be wandering through its rooms.

Historian Christoph Bull suggested one famous former guest as a possible identity for the man in the old fashioned hat, mentioned by Lucy.

Mr Bull, president of the Dartford Historical and Antiquarian Society, said he had heard rumours about the hotel being haunted, although he did not know the details of the sightings.

“I would imagine everyone will tell you Richard Trevithick probably haunts it,” he said. “He was probably one of the most famous people to die there.”

Trevithick was a Cornish engineer who pioneered high pressure steam power and developed an early steam locomotive.

After returning penniless from South America, he found work with the engineering company. J and E Hall in Dartford.

He was living at the Bull Hotel when he became ill with pneumonia and died there on April 22, 1833.

Could Trevithick be the man Lucy saw beneath the old fashioned hat? There is no way of knowing.

Christoph offered the suggestion with some humour, adding that Trevithick had at least paid his hotel bill before he died.

The hotel’s manager, Lewis Jarrett, said he had been a sceptic when he began working at the Royal Victoria and Bull 18 months ago.

After hearing accounts of its ghosts, he decided to try a Ouija board for fun with three friends.

They placed a glass on the board, rested their fingers lightly upon it and began asking whether anybody was present.

“I didn’t believe in it,” Lewis said. “I thought, ‘What if you are moving the glass with fingers?’”

The friends removed their fingers one at a time to test whether anybody was guiding it, but Lewis said the glass continued moving.

Again and again, it selected the letters E, S and Q and no one knew what this meant.

Later research revealed that on August 17, 1775, a wealthy Irishman called John Parker, Esq was shot in one of the rooms at the Bull.

Parker and his brother Francis owed about £3,000 to Joseph Stacpoole, an Irish barrister who believed they were preparing to flee abroad without repaying him.

Stacpoole travelled to the Bull with lawyer William Gapper and bailiff James Lagier, and entered Parker’s room carrying a writ connected with the debt.

Parker called for his pistols before one of his companions extinguished the lights, plunging the room into darkness.

Stacpoole was carrying a carbine, a compact lightweight firearm, which discharged during the confrontation, striking Parker with three bullets.

Despite his injuries, he survived.

The subsequent trial at Maidstone Assizes, law courts where several high-profile witchcraft trials also took place, was documented in a detailed 61 page account and the incident from March 20, 1777 was later retold by Charles G Harper in ‘The Old Inns of Old England’.

The Irish esquire survived his encounter at the Bull, but another man was not so fortunate.

According to Fred Roe’s 1907 book ‘Old Oak Furniture’, an unidentified man was murdered in one of the hotel’s rooms in 1773.

Three bullets reportedly passed through his body, leaving marks on the wall behind him.

The murder victim remained in the room overnight, awaiting examination by a coroner and an inquest the following morning.

When people returned, however, his body had disappeared.

To this day, nobody knows who the victim was, who killed him or what happened to his remains.

In early 1899, builders carrying out alterations to the pub uncovered an old oak chest concealed beneath the cellar floor.

Inside was the skeleton of a man.

The discovery raised the possibility that the remains belonged to the victim who vanished in 1773.

However, the skeleton was never identified and a connection between the two events could not be proved.

Three marks can still be seen on a wall in the hotel’s function room and are believed to have been left by the bullets used in the killing.

The Royal Victoria and Bull is believed to be Dartford’s oldest surviving inn.

The site is thought to have accommodated travellers since at least the 14th century, while the present Grade II* listed building dates from 1703.

Christoph said the meaning of its name is often misunderstood.

“The bull it refers to is not the one with horns,” he said. “It’s the papal bull,” referring to a formal document issued by the Pope.

The building and surrounding land once belonged to Dartford Priory.

But the nuns did not serve drinks or operate the establishment themselves.

Instead, they rented it to a publican who provided food, accommodation and fresh horses for travellers.

Passengers could rest in its rooms before continuing their journeys, while carriages passed through its entrance and horses were changed in the courtyard.

Traces of its coaching past remain today, including the carriage entrance, two long wings and galleries overlooking the former courtyard.

Queen Victoria herself spent a night at the hotel during February 1838 and after the name was changed into ‘Royal Victoria and the Bull’.

The hotel’s bedrooms are named after characters from Jane Austen’s novels, including Kitty Bennet, one of the five sisters in Pride and Prejudice.

The pub is also linked to tales of tea smuggled inside a stagecoach, forbidden love and many other secrets.

It’s not the only place in town to report frequent supernatural going-ons.

Less than 200 metres away is Dartford Museum which featured in a 2007 episode of Most Haunted.

During that investigation, presenter Yvette Fielding and her team claimed to encounter unexplained activity, including mysterious knocking sounds, books apparently falling from shelves and what Fielding described as a ghostly hand moving up her leg.

Anyone wishing to hear more about what The Paranormal Inspectres discovered can join them at the Royal Victoria and Bull on October 1 from 7pm onwards or visit their website.

Sue hopes people will come along to share their own experiences at the hotel and hear more about the spirits believed to inhabit its rooms as part of the free event.
